question: The fragmentation of the European electric vehicle charging market continues to create significant difficulties for consumers, particularly when travelling across Member States. Drivers may face different prices for the same charging session depending on whether they use an operator’s RFID card, a mobile application, a QR code or a bank card.

At the same time, Plug and Charge technology based on ISO 15118, which could considerably simplify charging by enabling automatic vehicle authentication and payment, remains insufficiently interoperable in practice.

Moreover, some vehicle manufacturers appear to restrict Plug and Charge functionality to their own charging or mobility services, potentially limiting consumer choice and disadvantaging competing providers. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission assess whether significant price differences between payment methods comply with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2023/18041 concerning reasonable, transparent, comparable and non-discriminatory prices?

What further measures will the Commission take to ensure that Plug and Charge is genuinely operational and interoperable across the EU, rather than merely technically supported by charging infrastructure?

Will the Commission consider measures preventing vehicle manufacturers from restricting Plug and Charge to proprietary charging or payment services, so as to ensure consumers can freely choose their preferred mobility service provider?

Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of 13 September 2023 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure, and repealing Directive 2014/94/EU (OJ L 234, 22.9.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1804/oj). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.10.2026) Regulation (EU) 2023/18041 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure (AFIR) requires that prices charged by operators of publicly accessible recharging points and mobility service providers are reasonable, transparent, comparable and non-discriminatory.

Article 5(6) AFIR specifically requires Member States to monitor the markets, in particular with regards to compliance with AFIR provisions on pricing. AFIR does not contain specific benchmarks for compliance with those provisions that need to be assessed on a case by case basis.

Under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/6562, new recharging points deployed from 1 January 2027 must comply with standard EN ISO 15118-20:2022, including for offering automatic authentication and authorisation services, such as plug and charge, ensuring an interoperable communication interface with electric vehicles. Genuine interoperability also requires a trusted governance and technical framework.

The Commission3 is currently developing the EU-wide framework needed to support interoperable, open and market-driven plug and charge services. Technical implementation is proceeding on a voluntary basis. The Commission will assess the need for further action when the project concludes in 2028. Manufacturer proprietary services could potentially limit consumer choice.
The Commission’s ongoing AFIR review will assess whether further measures are needed to protect drivers’ freedom of choice and ensure a level playing field for plug and charge services.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on the
deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure, and repealing Directive 2014/94/EU (OJ L 234, 22.9.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1804/oj).

2 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/656 of 2 April 2025 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards standards for wireless recharging, electric road system, vehicle-to-grid communication and hydrogen supply for road transport vehicles (OJ L, 2025/656, 18.6.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2025/656/oj).
